body:
**VICTORIA, B.C. — Sept. 27, 2026 —** It's day five of British Columbia's snap election campaign, and no party has released a full, costed platform yet. This is where things stand today, based on campaign announcements and each party's existing policy pages.

Premier David Eby called the election on Sept. 22 — about two years early — arguing that the Canada-U.S. trade fight means voters "deserve a say." Voting day is Saturday, Oct. 24. Advance voting runs Oct. 16–21, and Oct. 1 is the last day to register if you want your voter card mailed to you.

Early polls disagree on who's ahead: Angus Reid has the Conservatives at 43% and the NDP at 35%, while Liaison Strategies has the NDP at 41% and the Conservatives at 36%. Both put the Greens around 12%, with roughly one in five voters still undecided.

## BC NDP (David Eby)

The NDP is running mainly on standing up to Trump, warning that a Conservative government would bring cuts and private health care.

- **Housing:** A new tax on finished condos that sit unsold for more than a year, starting at 2%. The speculation and vacancy tax would rise to 2% for domestic owners and 5% for foreign owners.
- **Health care:** Triple the budget for recruiting U.S. health workers to $15 million, aiming for more than 2,400 hires.
- **Economy:** A push on major projects, including LNG, the North Coast Transmission Line, ports and trades training.
- **Indigenous rights law (DRIPA):** The NDP tried to amend the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act earlier this year and backed off after First Nations objected. Eby hasn't said what he'd do now.
- No campaign pledges have surfaced yet on public safety, education or climate.

## BC Conservatives (Lorne Doerkson, interim leader)

The party has released nothing formal yet. Its previous leader, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, resigned on Sept. 20 after 13 of her MLAs quit or were expelled.

- **DRIPA:** "I will repeal DRIPA." Doerkson calls this his top priority and says he'd work with First Nations directly on partnerships instead.
- **Budget:** He wants it balanced "immediately," through deregulation and productivity gains rather than cuts — though he admits he doesn't have a path worked out yet.
- **Trump:** He calls Trump "an absolute bully" and would keep American liquor off store shelves.
- He has named affordability, housing, health care, the economy and crime as priorities, with no specifics so far. A 20% income tax cut sometimes attributed to the party was one leadership candidate's idea, not official policy.

## BC Greens (Emily Lowan)

The Greens are aiming to hold the balance of power in a minority government.

- **Taxes** (announced October 2025): new top income tax brackets of 24%, 27% and 30% on income over $350K, $500K and $1M. They'd also bring in a one-time wealth tax on the ultra-rich, an inheritance tax on transfers over $5 million, a land value tax to replace property tax, a higher corporate rate, and an 18% tax on corporate profits above $1 billion.
- They also promise thousands of new social housing units and community health centres, and oppose new oil pipelines and tankers.

## CentreBC (Elenore Sturko, 1 MLA)

CentreBC has only general values published so far: balanced budgets over the long term, support for resource industries alongside green tech, and strong justice and treatment systems. Sturko is pitching the party to voters who feel unrepresented by either the NDP or the Conservatives.

## OneBC (Dallas Brodie, 2 MLAs)

OneBC has the most detailed policy page of any party, though nothing is costed:

- Repeal DRIPA, end transfers of land and control to band governments, and push to repeal the Indian Act.
- Cut every income tax bracket by 25% and take two points off the PST.
- Build an oil pipeline to the north coast.
- Allow private health care alongside public care.
- Remove SOGI 123 (the sexual orientation and gender identity school resources) and bring in standardized testing.
- End safe supply and consumption sites, and bring in involuntary rehab.

## Where they split hardest

DRIPA is the sharpest divide: the Conservatives and OneBC would repeal it, while the NDP's position is unclear. On taxes, the Greens would raise them on the wealthy, the NDP is targeting empty and speculative housing, and OneBC would cut across the board. On energy, the NDP backs LNG, OneBC wants an oil pipeline, and the Greens oppose both pipelines and tankers.

It's only day five of the campaign, so expect a lot more detail once full platforms and the debates arrive. The Green tax plan and the OneBC and CentreBC pages are standing policy, not documents launched for this election.
